source_refs.note: Book p. 112: 6.9.1 definition of H.M., derivation H = 2ab/(a+b), example H.M. of 3 and 7 = 21/5. Teaching notes, comparison of means, key points and common mistakes are ours.

blocks.text: A number \(H\) is said to be the harmonic mean (H.M.) between two numbers \(a\) and \(b\) if \(a, H, b\) are in H.P.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
A "mean between" two numbers is a number that fits in the middle so that the three numbers form a progression. For an A.P. this is the arithmetic mean \(A = \frac{a+b}{2}\), for a G.P. the geometric mean \(G = \pm\sqrt{ab}\). The harmonic mean is the middle number of an H.P.
Since an H.P. is an A.P. of reciprocals, \(\frac{1}{H}\) must be the arithmetic mean of \(\frac{1}{a}\) and \(\frac{1}{b}\). That is the whole derivation below.
Let \(a, b\) be the two numbers and \(H\) be their H.M. Then \(\frac{1}{a}, \frac{1}{H}, \frac{1}{b}\) are in A.P. Therefore,

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is \(\frac{1}{H}\) the average of \(\frac{1}{a}\) and \(\frac{1}{b}\)? In an A.P. the middle term is the same distance from both ends: \(\frac{1}{H} - \frac{1}{a} = \frac{1}{b} - \frac{1}{H}\). Adding \(\frac{1}{H} + \frac{1}{a}\) to both sides gives \(\frac{2}{H} = \frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b}\).
The middle step adds the two fractions with the common denominator \(ab\): \(\frac{1}{a} + \frac{1}{b} = \frac{b+a}{ab}\); dividing by \(2\) multiplies the denominator by \(2\).
and, taking the reciprocal of both sides,

For example, H.M. between \(3\) and \(7\) is

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Check that \(3, \frac{21}{5}, 7\) really are in H.P.: their reciprocals are \(\frac{1}{3}, \frac{5}{21}, \frac{1}{7}\), i.e. \(\frac{7}{21}, \frac{5}{21}, \frac{3}{21}\), which decrease by \(\frac{2}{21}\) each time: an A.P.
Compare the three means of \(3\) and \(7\): \(A = 5\), \(G = \sqrt{21} \approx 4.58\), \(H = \frac{21}{5} = 4.2\). For two positive numbers it is always true that \(A \ge G \ge H\), and \(G^{2} = AH\) (here \(5 \times 4.2 = 21\)). These two facts are ours, not printed here, but they help in exercise questions about A.M., G.M. and H.M. together.

blocks.caption: Our comparison of the three means

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(H\) is the H.M. of \(a\) and \(b\) when \(a, H, b\) are in H.P.
2. Then \(\frac{1}{H}\) is the A.M. of \(\frac{1}{a}\) and \(\frac{1}{b}\).
3. \(H = \frac{2ab}{a+b}\) (with \(a, b, a+b \ne 0\)).
4. For positive numbers: \(A \ge G \ge H\) and \(G^{2} = AH\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Writing \(H = \frac{a+b}{2ab}\): that is \(\frac{1}{H}\); remember to take the reciprocal at the end.
2. Writing \(\frac{2}{a+b}\) (forgetting the product \(ab\)) or \(\frac{ab}{a+b}\) (forgetting the \(2\)).
3. Thinking the H.M. is the reciprocal of the A.M. of \(a\) and \(b\): for \(3\) and \(7\) that would give \(\frac{1}{5}\), but the H.M. is \(\frac{21}{5}\).
